verdict.why: kaikki-it-en reads solo as /ˈso.lo/; the model wrote /ˈsɔ.lo/

notes: As an adjective, 'solo' changes its ending to match gender and number ('solo', 'sola', 'soli', 'sole'). Do not confuse it with the adverb 'solo' ('only'), which never changes form.
Often used in the phrase 'da solo' ('by oneself', 'on one's own'), which also agrees with the person: 'vivo da sola' (spoken by a woman).

examples.text: Oggi preferisco stare solo a casa.
examples.translation: Today I prefer to stay home alone.
examples.emotion: relaxed and content, choosing a quiet moment for oneself

senses.definition: Unhappy because of having no friends or company.

examples.text: A volte mi sento solo in questa grande città.
examples.translation: Sometimes I feel lonely in this big city.
examples.emotion: a bit melancholic and vulnerable, speaking from the heart

senses.definition: Being the only one; not more than one.

examples.text: C'è un solo biglietto rimasto per il concerto.
examples.translation: There is only a single ticket left for the concert.

notes: When 'solo' means 'alone' (as in 'I am alone'), it changes its ending based on the gender and number of the person: 'sono solo' (if you are male) or 'sono sola' (if you are female).
It is often confused with 'soltanto', which only means 'only'. If you want to say 'only one', use 'solo'. If you want to say 'only two minutes', you can use either 'solo' or 'soltanto'.
